reasons_add: Sībawayh says the interrogative hamza prevents the preceding verb from governing the internal nominal clause in 'which has purer food'; he contrasts a question beginning the complement, whose subject stays nominative, with an independently framed question later governed by a verb. He explains that araʾaytuka takes an accusative first object and the interrogative clause as its second object. His comparisons distinguish accusative adverbial 'which day' from nominative nonadverbial use, note Arabs' varying case for 'which time,' and cite a poetic 'in every state or time' as adverbial. Al-Itqān gives ʿinda as a separate example of a word used only adverbially or governed by min; this is general background on grammatical government, not a gloss on a word in this verse.
Sībawayh requires a predicate after the interrogative subject within this embedded question: the question cannot depend on what precedes it and must be completed by what follows.
